title: Detection of Social Media Accounts
summary: This detection strategy covers the compromise of social media accounts, where an adversary takes over a corporate or employee social identity to support later phishing and impersonation. It matters because a post or message from a trusted company account reaches customers and staff who would ignore the same message from an unknown sender, and because account takeover is visible in login telemetry long before the abuse becomes public. The telemetry that makes it possible is the platform audit log, the identity provider sign-in log with risk annotations and the email security gateway report of messages sent from your own domain. It fails in practice because many organisations do not queue social platform audit logs into the SIEM, so the only signal left is the phishing report that arrives after the abuse.

beginner.definition: A social media account compromise means someone else gains control of a company or staff account. The attacker can then post messages or send direct messages that look official. This detection looks for the first sign of that takeover in login records.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust messages from an account they already follow. That trust is exactly what an attacker wants. A single post can send many staff or customers to a fake login page. The takeover also damages the brand and takes time to undo. Login records usually show the takeover before any post appears.
howItWorks: The platform or the single sign on provider writes an audit record when someone signs in or changes account settings.
Those records are sent to your SIEM, together with the risk score the provider gives to each sign in.
The rule looks for a failed sign in burst followed by a success from a new address, a new device or an unusual country.
It also watches for changes right after that sign in, such as a new recovery address, a new application approval or a new administrator.
When the pattern appears, the alert names the account, the address and the change so the owner can be reached at once.
beginner.example: Think of a till receipt at a shop. The receipt shows who opened the register, at what time and what changed in the drawer. If a register is opened at three in the morning by a staff card that belongs to someone on holiday, the receipt is enough to start asking questions.
takeaways: A takeover shows up as an unusual sign in long before the first malicious post.
Risk scoring from the identity provider is a strong signal, but it must be routed into your SIEM.
Fast containment matters more than perfect detection here, because each minute of access can reach the audience.

objectives: Explain why a trusted social identity is valuable to an adversary
List the audit events that show a social account has changed hands
Correlate identity provider risk scores with account setting changes in the same session
Configure alerting that reaches the account owner and the communications team quickly
Define a containment checklist for a confirmed social account takeover
dataSources: Social platform audit logs showing sign in location, device, password reset and permission changes
Cloud identity provider sign in logs with risk level, conditional access result and multi factor outcome
Email security gateway records of messages sent from your domain to external recipients
Help desk records of user reports about unexpected posts or messages from a company account
logic: The pattern is a chain of identity events on one account inside a short window: several failed sign ins, then a success from an address or device the account has never used, followed by a security setting change such as a new recovery address, a new application consent or a new delegated administrator. The fields to correlate are the account identity, the source address, the device or user agent, the risk level and the type of change. The benign case is a user who signs in from a new place but keeps the same device and does not change recovery settings, while the malicious case bundles a new location with a recovery change and immediate outbound messaging.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Social account sign in from new location followed by setting change
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: signin
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type:
#       - password_reset
#       - recovery_email_added
#       - app_consent_granted
#       - new_device_registered
#   risk:
#     - medium
#     - high
#   filter:
#     source_ip|in: corporate_vpn_ranges
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: A marketing team member travelling abroad who signs in from a hotel network and adds a personal recovery address
An employee replacing a lost phone, which registers a new device and resets multi factor settings
A social media management tool that signs in on behalf of the brand account from a cloud address
A password manager or single sign on application that triggers a fresh consent prompt after an update
tuningNotes: Filter out your corporate virtual private network ranges and the published addresses of approved social media management tools, then baseline the usual sign in countries and user agents per account over a month. Scope the highest severity tier to brand, executive and communications accounts, where the audience impact is largest. You lose early warning for ordinary employee accounts, so keep a medium tier for them with a longer correlation window and review it daily instead of in real time.
